items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

items.title: [tuoitre.vn] European Hera probe begins examining asteroid struck in NASA deflection test
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun surveying the Didymos asteroid pair from about 25 to 30 kilometers away, four years after NASA deliberately struck the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, to test asteroid deflection. Hera’s first images show Didymos from a new angle, revealing boulders, craters and ridge-like features; some rocks may have been blasted from Dimorphos and traveled about 1 kilometer to the larger asteroid. The 2022 impact shortened Dimorphos’ orbit around Didymos by about 32 to 33 minutes and also altered the pair’s path around the sun. Hera’s close-up investigation aims to determine how the impact changed Dimorphos and why the deflection was greater than simulations predicted. The probe is expected to begin closer, more detailed observations next month, using 25 instruments and two CubeSats that will survey Dimorphos and attempt to land there.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] Powerful El Niño nears December peak as droughts, fires threaten crops
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization says the powerful El Niño underway in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and likely persist through February 2027, disrupting rainfall and raising drought and flood risks worldwide. Sea-surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region rose from 1.6°C above normal in June to 2.5°C above normal in August; forecasters project temperatures about 3.7°C above normal in October-December, exceeding the previous record of 2.6°C above normal. Recent impacts include drought and fires in Brazil, extensive forest fires in Indonesia, and a possible 21% to 25% decline in Ivory Coast cocoa output. Researchers attributed Indonesia’s July-October rainfall deficit largely to El Niño, while saying human-caused climate change made the atmospheric conditions about three times more likely and more intense. The United Nations Development Programme says acting now to limit the impacts would cost $36 billion, compared with $73 billion if action is delayed.

These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

items.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

Reports describe deadly glacier flooding in Nepal and wildfires in Europe. Australia released the text on Nov. 16 for negotiations among nearly 200 countries; it includes competing proposals to “transition away” from fossil fuels or phase them out, but either could be removed before an agreement is reached. The draft also proposes at least $120 billion a year for adaptation in developing countries by 2035. Climate campaigners say it lacks a clear process for advancing fossil-fuel roadmaps and that the proposed funding would cover less than a third of estimated needs. The proposed electricity target has also drawn criticism because the text does not require the added power to come from renewable sources. Negotiators must reach consensus before the summit’s scheduled close on Nov. 20. Australia’s climate change and energy minister and lead negotiator, Chris Bowen, expects further revisions as ministers negotiate the disputed language.

items.title: [kyivindependent.com] Regulators warn Russian grid strikes put Ukraine’s reactors at risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

International nuclear safety regulators representing 38 countries warned on Nov. 16 that attacks on Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure are increasing the risk of a nuclear accident this winter. The three groups behind the statement—the Western European Nuclear Regulators Association, the Heads of European Radiological Protection Competent Authorities and the Heads of Nordic Radiation Safety Authorities—called on Russia to stop attacks on nuclear facilities and the power network needed to operate them safely. Ukraine’s three operating nuclear plants have nine generating reactors and supply about 80% of the country’s electricity this winter. The plants also need a stable power supply to run cooling and other safety systems. The International Atomic Energy Agency said military activity disrupted the grid in the week before Nov. 14, forcing some units to reduce output. The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant is not generating electricity but needs external power to cool its nuclear material. It has lost off-site power 27 times since the war began and has relied on one external line since late March. Per Strand, who heads two of the regulatory groups, warned that a nationwide blackout could affect all nine operating reactors simultaneously and urged European countries to coordinate emergency preparations if attacks continue. International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi has called for an end to military operations against electricity infrastructure linked to nuclear safety and urged both sides to keep working with the agency.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes (arstechnica.com, techspot.com, theregister.com). The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act (pcmag.com, theregister.com). The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028 (arstechnica.com). First locations: The five upgraded sites are Atlantic City, Nashville and Greater Rochester international airports, plus FAA data-processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City (techspot.com, pcmag.com). Systems replaced: E-IDS will replace IDS-4, ACE-IDS, NIDS and ERIDS, which separately provide weather, airport, airspace and en-route flight information (arstechnica.com, theregister.com). Safety record: A 2023 NOTAM system failure following the accidental deletion of a file temporarily halted domestic flight departures nationwide (theregister.com). Funding gap: The FAA says the proposed Modern Skies Act would provide $30 billion for modernization. A September Government Accountability Office report said the overhaul’s second phase needed a further $10.2 billion and had no completion date (theregister.com).
